title: Remembering What It's Like To Be A Student
author: Blake Harvard
summary: Blake Harvard opens with a five-minute video of his son teaching viewers to solve a Rubik's Cube, then asks readers to honestly assess whether they could now solve one, describe the steps, or earn a good grade on the skill -- almost certainly not, despite having watched and listened attentively. He uses this to illustrate how cognitively demanding it is for students to process genuinely new material after a single exposure, something teachers, who already possess deep fluency in their subject, systematically underestimate. Harvard names this the 'curse of knowledge': because he has taught the same course for 13 years and understands the material fluently, he can effortlessly connect new information to what he already knows, but he shouldn't expect students -- encountering it for the first time -- to do the same. He closes by urging teachers to set moderate expectations for student success until material has been retrieved and applied multiple times, arguing this both normalizes forgetting and models better learning strategies.
points: Harvard's Rubik's Cube demonstration makes the curse of knowledge experiential for the reader rather than purely conceptual -- readers who just watched a competent tutorial and still can't perform the skill directly feel the gap between exposure and mastery.

His self-diagnostic trigger phrase -- 'I taught this yesterday, I understand it, why don't my students get it?' -- gives teachers a concrete internal cue for catching themselves mid-curse-of-knowledge.

Harvard connects the curse of knowledge to unconscious, unfair expectation-setting: teachers assume a shared foundation of knowledge with students that doesn't actually exist, and frustration follows when students don't meet that assumption.

His practical recommendation -- set moderate expectations for success until content has been retrieved and used multiple times -- reframes early struggle as expected and normal rather than evidence of a failed lesson.
quotes: It is so incredibly difficult to listen to a concept that you have little knowledge of, retain that information, and use it appropriately when needed…especially when you’ve only attended to that content once.
Sometimes we forget what it’s like to be a student. We forget what it’s like to sit in a classroom and experience terms and concepts that are totally new.
Teachers, or really anyone with a firm grasp of any particular domain of knowledge, are especially susceptible to displaying the curse of knowledge.
Humans are unfortunately vulnerable to assuming others have a shared foundation of knowledge and set expectations based on this bias.
Until your students have had numerous experiences hearing, seeing, and applying the material, should they be expected to know how to use it correctly? I'm not so sure.
Not only does this create an environment that normalizes forgetting and makes it acceptable to try and fail and try again, it also models for students more effective learning strategies.
